## Paper

## Abstract

Photocatalytic four-component reaction is an efficient and environmentally friendly synthetic strategy known for its step economy and operational simplicity, enabling the preparation of diverse organic products. However, its application in synthesizing covalent organic frameworks (COFs) remains unexplored. Here, we report the rational synthesis of a class of functionalized COFs with high crystallinity and permanent porosity via the photocatalytic four-component reaction. This strategy not only addresses the long-standing challenge of harsh reaction conditions in conventional COFs synthesis methods, but also enables the integration of four different types of monomers in a one-pot process to create structurally diverse COFs. Furthermore, the resulting Cp-tBu-N3-COF can function as an efficient photocatalyst for the visible-light-driven synthesis of benzimidazoles. This work provides a promising strategy to access COFs in a mild and sustainable way.

---

## Introduction

Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are a class of crystalline, porous organic polymers with highly ordered and extended structures, known for their intriguing properties of tunable pore size, large surface area, high chemical stability, and easy recyclability1–7. Since Yaghi et al. reported the synthesis of COFs in 20058, considerable progress has been made in their synthesis over the past 20 years9–14. However, most of the reported methods rely on relatively harsh reaction conditions, such as high temperature and pressure, underscoring the need for novel strategies to prepare COFs under mild conditions.

Visible-light photoredox catalysis has emerged as a powerful approach in synthetic chemistry for the synthesis of complex molecules from simple starting materials because of its mildness, low-energy consumption, and environmental friendliness15–20. Its versatility has also been demonstrated in providing alternative routes for the construction of COFs. Compared with the conventional methods for COFs synthesis, photoredox catalysis enables the formation of COFs under mild reaction conditions, while only a few examples have been reported thus far21–24. Research on the photocatalytic synthesis of COFs is still in the early stage, and its potential remains largely unexploited. Therefore, it is highly desirable yet challenging to explore more photocatalytic reactions to provide more possibilities in the design and preparation of COFs.

Multicomponent reactions (MCRs), which involve the one-pot combination of at least three substrates to form multiple new bonds without separating intermediates, are recognized as powerful tools in synthetic chemistry25,26. These reactions are valued for their convenient operation, high efficiency, and structural diversity. Recently, different types of MCRs, particularly three-component reactions such as Debus−Radziszewski reaction, Strecker reaction, Povarov reaction, and thiazole formation reaction, have been successfully applied to construct various COFs27–37. Despite these advances, the extension to four-component reactions (4CRs)38 for COFs synthesis remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the significantly increased complexity in controlling regio- and chemoselectivity. To date, Wang and co-workers reported the only case of the synthesis of functionalized COFs via the 4CRs using the solvothermal method39, which represents a major advancement in this field. This achievement highlights the potential of 4CRs to assemble four distinct monomers in a one-pot process, enabling the construction of structurally diverse COFs. When comparing various synthetic strategies, although the conventional two-component method is operationally simple and straightforward, it has fundamental limitations in terms of structural complexity and functional integration. The three-component reaction can offer improved structural diversity, yet remains constrained by relatively limited combinations of building blocks. In contrast, 4CRs offer a greater variety of combinatorial possibilities and allow precise integration of multiple functional groups within a single framework. The development of 4CRs systems will not only broaden the structural diversity of COFs, but also promote the advancement of their applications.

Given the immense potential of both 4CRs and photocatalysis, we propose integrating these two strategies to synthesize functionalized COFs via a photocatalytic four-component reaction—an approach that has yet to be explored. The merger of 4CRs with visible-light photoredox catalysis to synthesize functionalized COFs represents a significant advancement in the field of porous material synthesis. Firstly, it fully exploited the significant potential of the four-component reactions in achieving structural diversity and functional integration. Secondly, the implementation of photocatalytic technology effectively overcomes the limitations imposed by the conventional harsh reaction conditions. Finally, this photocatalytic four-component reaction strategy will open up new avenues for constructing COFs that are otherwise inaccessible through conventional methods.

Herein, we introduce a photocatalytic four-component reaction strategy for COFs synthesis at room temperature. Under visible-light irradiation, a series of COFs with high crystallinity and permanent porosity are successfully constructed via the photocatalytic four-component reaction of aromatic aldehydes, hydrazines, aromatic olefins, and boronic acids, using 4CzIPN as the photocatalyst. Furthermore, the obtained Cp-tBu-N3-COF exhibits good photocatalytic activity in the visible-light-driven condensation-cyclization reaction to afford various benzimidazoles, which are valuable heterocyclic structures valued for their diverse pharmacological and biological activities. This clean-energy-triggered approach not only offers a solution to the problem of harsh conditions in traditional synthetic methods but also allows the precise synthesis of structurally diverse COFs through the one-pot integration of four different types of monomers.

---

## Results

Synthesis of Cp-tBu-N3-COF
As illustrated in Fig. 1a, the model reaction involving aniline, benzaldehyde, 4-tert-butylstyrene, and cyclopentylboronic acid successfully produced the model compound of M in 87% yield (Supplementary Figs. 2, 3)40. Based on this, we performed the photocatalytic four-component reaction by condensing four types of monomers, including 2,4,6-tris(4-formylphenyl)-1,3,5-triazine (TFTP), hydrazine (HZ), 4-tert-butylstyrene (tBs), and cyclopentylboronic acid (CpBa). The synthetic conditions were systematically optimized by screening key parameters, including the acid, solvent, photocatalyst, light source, gas atmosphere, and reaction time (Supplementary Figs. 4–7). The optimized conditions were determined as crystallization in 1,4-dioxane/n-BuOH/DMA mixture (1.5:0.5:0.3, v/v/v) with acetic acid as the catalyst and 4CzIPN as the photocatalyst, under visible-light irradiation at room temperature for 72 h. Under the optimized conditions, the Cp-tBu-N3-COF was obtained as a yellow solid in 72% yield (Fig. 1b).

Characterization of COFs
Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy, 13C CP-MAS solid-state NMR, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were employed to confirm the formation of Cp-tBu-N3-COF. In the FT-IR spectra of Cp-tBu-N3-COF, the characteristic peaks of 1704 cm−1 for C=O and 3356 cm−1 for N-H were strongly diminished after polymerization (Supplementary Fig. 8). In addition, compared to the pristine imine-based N3-COF41, the peak at approximately 1622 cm−1 corresponding to the C=N stretch was strongly attenuated, while new peaks appeared at 2864 and 2908 cm−1, associated with the cyclopentyl species, and at 2955 cm−1, corresponding to the tert-butyl group (Fig. 2a), indicating the successful formation of Cp-tBu-N3-COF. In the 13C CP-MAS solid-state NMR spectrum of Cp-tBu-N3-COF, resonance signals at 67, 31 and 25 ppm were observed, assigned to the carbons in C-NH, tert-butyl, and cyclopentyl moieties, respectively (Fig. 2b). Compared with N3-COF, the signal at 162 ppm corresponding to the imine carbon was significantly weakened, which provided solid evidence for the successful conversion of the imine linkage (Supplementary Fig. 9). XPS analysis further validated the chemical states of linked N atoms in Cp-tBu-N3-COF (Supplementary Fig. 10), revealing N 1s peaks at 398.9 and 398.2 eV, which are attributed to nitrogen in the C-NH bond and nitrogen in the triazine ring, respectively. All the spectral data are consistent with previous literature22,39 and the model compound (Supplementary Figs. 2, 3), confirming the successful synthesis of Cp-tBu-N3-COF.

As shown in Fig. 2c, the powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) analysis indicates that the obtained Cp-tBu-N3-COF is a highly crystalline material. The PXRD pattern features a series of peaks at 3.52°, 6.14°, 7.10°, and 9.40°, which can be attributed to the reflections of (100), (110), (200), and (210) planes, respectively. The PXRD pattern of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was simulated utilizing the software of Materials Studio (ver. 2018), indicating a 2D eclipsed (AA) stacking mode. This assignment was further confirmed by Pawley refinement, which showed good agreement between the simulated and experimental patterns. The Cp-tBu-N3-COF is assigned to the space group P6, with the optimized parameters of a=b=28.68 Å, c=6.10 Å, α=β=90°, γ=120°, residuals Rwp = 4.40%, and Rp = 3.32%. Based on crystal structure analysis, the eclipsed 2D structure of Cp-tBu-N3-COF contains hexagonal pores (d = ca. 1.4 nm) with an interlayer distance determined as ca. 6.10 Å (Fig. 2d).

The porosity of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was analyzed using N2 adsorption-desorption measurements at 77 K (Fig. 3a). The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area was determined to be 392 m2 g−1, with a total pore volume (P/P0 = 0.99) of 0.28 cm3 g−1. The pore size distribution, calculated using nonlocal density functional theory (NLDFT), revealed an average pore width of ~1.35 nm. This value agrees well with the pore size calculated from the simulated crystal structure, further confirming the validity of the simulated structure for Cp-tBu-N3-COF. In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was employed to observe the morphology of Cp-tBu-N3-COF, which showed a micrometer-scale particle morphology (Supplementary Fig. 11). The high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image of Cp-tBu-N3-COF clearly showed the ordered crystalline lattice fringes with an interplanar distance of 0.61 nm (Supplementary Fig. 11), which agreed well with the vertical interlayer spacing of the simulated models. These results confirmed the highly crystalline and ordered porous structure of Cp-tBu-N3-COF.

The thermal stability of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was evaluated using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), which revealed that the material remains stable up to 200 °C (Fig. 3b). Furthermore, in situ variable-temperature PXRD patterns for Cp-tBu-N3-COF were measured. The peaks remained unchanged before 200 °C (Supplementary Fig. 12), indicating no thermal degradation of the crystalline structure within this temperature range, which was also consistent with the TGA results. Subsequently, its chemical stability was further assessed by immersing it in 6 M sodium hydroxide (NaOH), 6 M hydrochloric acid (HCl), or ethanol (EtOH) for 3 days. The PXRD patterns and FT-IR spectra recorded after treatment remained almost identical to those of the pristine Cp-tBu-N3-COF, confirming its good chemical stability. Furthermore, Cp-tBu-N3-COF was found to be stable under blue LEDs irradiation, ensuring its suitability and reliability for photocatalysis (Fig. 3c, d).

The absorption property and energy levels of Cp-tBu-N3-COF were determined by the solid-state UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectrum and Mott–Schottky measurement (Fig. 4). The solid-state UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectrum of Cp-tBu-N3-COF displayed a broad absorption band extending up to 450 nm (Fig. 4a). The optical band gap (Eg) calculated from the Tauc plots was 2.80 eV (Fig. 4b), indicating its semiconductor characteristics. The positive slopes of the Mott–Schottky plots suggested that Cp-tBu-N3-COF was a kind of n-type semiconductor (Fig. 4c). The flat band of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was 0.04 V vs. RHE, and the conduction band (CB) was 0.04 V vs. RHE. Integrating the optical band gap and CB potential, the valence band (VB) was determined to be 2.84 V vs. RHE (Fig. 4d). Because the CB of Cp-tBu-N3-COF is more negative than the reduction potential of O2/O2•− (0.12 V vs. RHE), it can thermodynamically drive photocatalytic organic transformations mediated by O2•−. Furthermore, the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and photocurrent response were also investigated (Supplementary Fig. 13). Cp-tBu-N3-COF exhibited a small Nyquist radius and strong transient photocurrent response, indicating its small charge-transfer resistance and high photogenerated carriers transport efficiency. All the obtained results demonstrated that Cp-tBu-N3-COF could act as a promising photocatalyst.

Photocatalytic activity of Cp-tBu-N3-COF
Benzimidazole derivatives are important heterocyclic organic compounds with notable pharmacological and biological activities42. Their synthesis was chosen as a probe reaction to evaluate the photocatalytic performance of the synthesized Cp-tBu-N3-COF. The photocatalytic oxidative cyclization of o-phenylenediamine (1a) and benzaldehyde (2a) served as a model reaction. When a mixture of the substrates and a catalytic amount of Cp-tBu-N3-COF in acetone was irradiated by blue LEDs (λ = 440 nm) in air at room temperature for 8 h, the desired product, 2-phenylbenzimidazole (3a), was obtained in 26% yield (Table 1, entry 1). The effect of different solvents on the reaction yield was investigated, and EtOH was identified as the optimal solvent, affording 3a in a high yield of 97% (Table 1, entries 2–6). Screening of photocatalyst loading showed that 6 mg of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was optimal to yield 3a in 97% (Table 1, entries 6–8). When irradiated by LEDs of different wavelengths (Table 1, entries 9 and 10), no improvement in yield was observed compared to blue LEDs. Furthermore, the photocatalytic activity of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was competitive with that of most of the reported heterogeneous photocatalysts for this reaction (Supplementary Table 2). The photocatalytic activity of Cp-tBu-N3-COF was further quantified, with an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of 0.46% and a turnover frequency (TOF) of 4.39 h⁻¹ (performed once). Control experiments conducted without Cp-tBu-N3-COF, visible light, or oxygen resulted in only trace amounts of product, highlighting their indispensable roles in the catalytic system (Table 1, entries 11–13). Thus, the optimized conditions for this reaction were determined to be: 0.2 mmol of 1a, 0.2 mmol of 2a, and 6 mg of Cp-tBu-N3-COF in 2 mL of EtOH, irradiated with blue LEDs (λ = 440 nm) in air for 8 h at room temperature (Table 1, entry 6).

The leaching test shows that Cp-tBu-N3-COF is a typical heterogeneous catalyst (Fig. 5a). As reusability of a photocatalyst in heterogeneous reactions is a prime merit for industrial applications, a recycling experiment was conducted, and the yield of 3a remained as high as 95% even after five catalytic cycles (Fig. 5b). Moreover, the PXRD patterns and FT-IR spectra of Cp-tBu-N3-COF before and after five cycles are almost identical, indicating that its crystallinity and chemical structure were largely preserved (Fig. 5c, d). These results demonstrate that Cp-tBu-N3-COF has good photocatalytic performance and recyclability, making it a promising photocatalyst in photocatalysis.

With the optimal reaction conditions established, we further explored the scope of the benzimidazole formation reaction, as summarized in Table 2. A series of aromatic aldehydes with electron-donating or electron-withdrawing substituents were efficiently converted to substituted benzimidazoles in good yields, albeit some steric hindrance effect (3a–3n). Heterocyclic aldehydes, including 4-pyridinecarboxaldehyde and thiophene-3-carbaldehyde also performed well, yielding the corresponding benzimidazoles in 88% and 86% yields, respectively (3o–3p). In addition, the aliphatic substrate cyclohexanecarboxaldehyde was found to be highly effective, affording the product in 90% yield (3q). Similarly, various aromatic diamines bearing the substituents (–F, –Cl, and –Me) on the phenyl ring were converted to the desired benzimidazoles in high yields (3r–3u).

The photocatalytic process was significantly hindered under a nitrogen atmosphere, highlighting the crucial role of oxygen in the reaction (Table 1, entry 13). It is hypothesized that O2•− plays a key role in this photocatalytic process. To confirm the presence of reactive oxygen species during the reaction, a series of controlled experiments were conducted. p-Benzoquinone and NaN3 were added to the reaction system as capturing agents for O2•− and 1O2, respectively. The introduction of p-benzoquinone resulted in a sharp decrease of the yield from 97% to 26%, while NaN3 only slightly reduced the yield (Table 1, entries 14 and 15), suggesting that O2•− was the important intermediate in this photocatalytic reaction, rather than 1O2. Furthermore, electron-spin resonance (ESR) experiments were conducted using 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) as an O2•− scavenger. The characteristic signal of O2•− captured by DMPO was clearly observed after irradiation with the blue LEDs (Supplementary Fig. 15), providing direct evidence of the involvement of O2•− in the transformation. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) computations were applied to visualize the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of the segment of Cp-tBu-N3-COF (Supplementary Fig. 16 and Supplementary Data 1). The HOMO and LUMO of the segment are mainly located at the hydrazine unit and the triazine moiety, respectively, suggesting the possibility of intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) within the framework, which may facilitate a single-electron transfer process. These computational results are thus consistent with the observed ability of Cp-tBu-N3-COF to generate superoxide anion radicals (O2•−) from triplet oxygen under visible light irradiation. The DFT method is inherently limited by the static nature of the simulations, which cannot fully capture the dynamic behavior under actual photocatalytic conditions.

Based on the above findings and previous reports43,44, a possible reaction mechanism is proposed (Fig. 6). Initially, 1a reacts with 2a via a Shiff-base reaction to form the imine intermediate I, which undergoes intramolecular cyclization to form intermediate II. At the same time, Cp-tBu-N3-COF reaches its excited state, Cp-tBu-N3-COF*, upon irradiation by visible light. This excited state is reductively quenched by intermediate II via a single electron transfer process to generate intermediate III and Cp-tBu-N3-COF•−. Subsequently, Cp-tBu-N3-COF•− is oxidized by molecular oxygen to produce O2•−, accompanied by the regeneration of Cp-tBu-N3-COF. Finally, the deprotonation and dehydrogenation of intermediate III assisted by O2•− affords the desired benzimidazole product 3a, and H2O2 as a byproduct.

The generality of this methodology for COFs synthesis
To further demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of the photocatalytic four-component reaction in constructing functionalized COFs, we synthesized three additional COFs, including Cy-tBu-N3-COF, Cy-OMe-N3-COF and Cp-F-N3-COF, using other different monomers under the same synthetic conditions (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Figs. 17–46).

AQY and TOF measurements
The apparent quantum yield (AQY) was calculated according to the formula47:
AQY(%) = (Number of reacted electrons / Number of incident photons) × 100% = (n(product) × NA × h × c / I × S × t × λ) × 100% (1)
where n(product) is the mole number of product (1.94 × 10−4 mol), NA is Avogadro’s number (6.02 × 1023 mol−1), h is Planck’s constant (6.626 × 10−34 J·s), c is the speed of light (3 × 108 ms−1), I is the light intensity (200 mW cm−2), S is the area of irradiation (2.0 cm2), t is irradiation time (8 h), and λ is the light wavelength (440 nm).

The turnover frequency (TOF) was calculated according to the formula48:
TOF = n(product) / (n(catalyst) × t) (2)
where n(product) is the mole number of product (0.194 mmol), n(catalyst) is the mole number of catalyst (0.0055 mmol), t is reaction time (8 h).

The working electrode was modified by drop-casting a suspension containing 0.2 mg of COF and 0.7 mg of carbon black in 50 µL of 5% Nafion solution. Mott-Schottky test was recorded in 0.5 M Na₂SO₄ solution (pH = 7.62 ± 0.03) at alternating current frequencies of 2000 Hz, 2500 Hz, and 3000 Hz. EIS measurements were conducted in a 0.1 M KCl electrolyte containing 5 mM K4[Fe(CN)₆]/K3[Fe(CN)₆]. All potentials were not iR corrected and were adjusted to the RHE reference scale using the formula:
ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.0591pH + 0.197 (3)

### Reviewer 1

This study reports the synthesis of a novel covalent organic framework (COF) via a photocatalytic four-component reaction
(4CR) and its application in the visible-light-driven synthesis of benzimidazoles. By integrating photocatalysis with
multicomponent reaction strategies, this work introduces an innovative and mild approach for COF synthesis. However, the
logical structure of the manuscript is not well emphasized, and the characterization methods require further depth and
refinement. Therefore, a major revision is recommended.

is recommended to adjust the logical focus of the article to better highlight the novelty of the study.
2. The introduction lacks a comprehensive comparison of existing three-component reactions (3CR), four-component

this work.

parameters such as catalyst type, solvent, light source, gas atmosphere, and reaction time.
4. PXRD data indicate that the COF exhibits high crystallinity. However, the c value of the unit cell is abnormally high. It is
suggested to include a schematic representation of the interlayer stacking mode of the COF structure.

PXRD data for consistency verification.
6. In Figure S2, the assignments of the solid-state NMR peaks should be clearly labeled. Additionally, the peak around 160

turnover frequency (TOF).
